all_of: a reverse proxy in front answers its OWN error page for some paths while the application answers for others, so the two can be told apart by the body
the proxy matches paths as literal strings and does not resolve dot segments or collapse a leading double slash, while the backend framework does
at least one rule the proxy enforces is security-relevant: an access denial, a rate limit, or both
the application has no registration, so the only way in is through the login query or the credentials behind it
any_of: a second factor short enough to enumerate
the second factor's pending state lives on the server with no cookie, so it is not bound to the client that logged in

chain.action: separate the two servers by their error pages before anything else: request a path that certainly does not exist and one that the navigation links to. Here /nope-xyz returned the Werkzeug 404 and /auth/login returned 403 with the body 'Request forbidden by administrative rules.'
chain.why: two different error formats means two different programs answering, and the one answering 403 is in front. That single observation turns 'the login is broken' into 'a proxy has a rule for this exact path', which is a completely different investigation

chain.action: map the proxy's rule set by asking which paths it answers for: sweep candidate routes and sort the replies by WHICH server produced them. The proxy answered for /auth/login and /dashboard; everything else fell through to Flask's 404
chain.why: a proxy rule is a signpost. The application has no link to /dashboard anywhere, and the only reason to know the route exists is that something in front bothered to deny it

chain.action: vary the path shape, not the path: //auth/login, /./auth/login, /auth/./login and /auth%2flogin all returned the login page, while /auth/login and /auth/login/ stayed 403
chain.why: HAProxy compares the literal request path. Werkzeug resolves dot segments and a leading double slash before routing, so every form that means the same route to the backend means a different string to the proxy

chain.action: with the login reachable, test the query behind it: username="admin' --" answered 302 to /auth/verify-2fa while username="admin' AND '1'='1" answered 400
chain.why: that pair is the whole diagnosis. The comment form succeeds because it removes the password clause, and the balanced-quote form fails because it leaves it in, so the password is in the same statement and the injection point is the username. It also hands over a boolean oracle: 302 is TRUE, 400 is FALSE

chain.action: extract with that oracle: sqlite_master has only users and sqlite_sequence, users has id, username, password and exactly one row, and the password is stored in plaintext
chain.why: reading the schema first is what proves the second factor is NOT in the database, which is the fact that decides the next step. A 2FA code the query cannot reach has to be attacked another way

chain.action: the rate limit has TWO independently attackable keys, and the handout shows both. haproxy.cfg:21 decides WHETHER to track with `acl is_auth_verify_2fa path_beg,url_dec /auth/verify-2fa`, and haproxy.cfg:32 decides WHICH BUCKET with `http-request track-sc0 hdr(X-Forwarded-For)`. Defeat either: //auth/verify-2fa never matches the ACL, so nothing is tracked; or keep the exact path and send a different X-Forwarded-For each time, so every request lands in its own bucket. Then brute-force the four digits and use the session on //dashboard
chain.why: the converter on line 21 drops path_beg's implicit -m beg and degrades the prefix match to an exact string compare -- the HAProxy 2.8.x bug this toolkit first measured on LockTalk, confirmed here on 2.8.3. The bucket key is worse: it is a header the client sends, and line 18 only supplies one when the request has none. Measured as four concurrent 40-request bursts: exact path with no header gave 20x400 then 14x429, rotating the header gave 40x400 and no 429 at all, a second no-header control gave 38x429 proving the bucket was still hot, and the doubled slash gave 39x400

first_confirming_probe.request: GET /auth/login and GET //auth/login with curl --path-as-is, and compare the bodies rather than only the status codes
first_confirming_probe.expected: the first returns a 403 whose body is the proxy's own page ('Request forbidden by administrative rules.'), the second returns the application's login form
first_confirming_probe.falsifier: both return the same error page, or the 403 body is in the application's own error format -- then the denial is the app's and no path trick can move it

blast_radius: The brute force is the dangerous part on a shared instance. The pending login is SERVER-SIDE with no cookie, so every attempt runs against state shared by everyone on that instance: a successful guess consumes it for whoever else was mid-login, and the traffic is thousands of requests in a burst. Keep the pool small, batch it, and stop at the first hit -- this solve stopped after 438 codes. The SQL injection is read-only as used here (a SELECT in the login), but the same injection point reaches an UPDATE-free statement only by luck, so do not extend it with stacked queries. Nothing was written to the target and nothing needs cleaning up.

verification.evidence: Live HTB instance. /auth/login -> 403 'Request forbidden by administrative rules.' while //auth/login -> 200 with <form action="/auth/login" method="POST">; username="admin' --" -> 302 location /auth/verify-2fa; the boolean oracle read users = 1:admin:<32-char plaintext password>; /auth/verify-2fa gave 20x400 then 10x429 while //auth/verify-2fa gave 30x400; code 0438 answered 302 to /dashboard with session=eyJhdXRoZW50aWNhdGVkIjp0cnVlfQ..., and //dashboard with that cookie returned 'Welcome, here is your flag: HTB{...}'. Recorded in challenges/wizardshop/state.json through tools/hooks.py post-probe (confirms, evidence-kind class three times then impact) and pre-flag (source live-response). Handout received AFTER the solve and read against it: blueprints/login.py:28 is the f-string SQL, login.py:10-14 is set_2fa_code(4) writing random.choices(string.digits, k=4) into one global uwsgi cache key for 300s, verify2fa.py:8 is the redirect that explains the lapse, verify2fa.py:26-29 is the race that explains the 500s, and conf/haproxy.cfg:21/32/36 are the three rules. Dockerfile pins haproxy 2.8.3. The rate-limit mechanism in step 6 was CORRECTED against the source and then re-measured: four concurrent 40-request bursts gave 20x400+14x429 (exact path, no header), 40x400 (exact path, rotating header), 38x429 (no-header control proving the bucket was hot) and 39x400 (doubled slash).

reuse_when: two different error-page formats come back from one host: that is a proxy in front, and the paths it answers for are the paths it has rules about. Map them before reading a single line of application logic
a route nothing links to answers 403 from the proxy: the proxy has just told you the route exists and matters. /dashboard was found this way, not by wordlist
any proxy-enforced access rule on a named path: try //path, /./path, /path/./x, /path%2f and a trailing slash, with curl --path-as-is. The proxy compares strings; the framework resolves them

a proxy-enforced RATE LIMIT: read it as TWO questions, not one. What decides that tracking happens (usually a path ACL), and what the counter is keyed on (usually a header). Either one is a bypass, and a header-keyed bucket is the weaker of the two because the client supplies it

any HAProxy stick-table tracked on hdr(X-Forwarded-For), X-Real-IP or a similar client-supplied value: rotate it. A rule that adds the header only `if !{ req.hdr(X-Forwarded-For) -m found }` hands the key straight to the attacker

a *_beg, *_end or *_sub ACL with a converter appended (path_beg,url_dec / path_beg,lower): on HAProxy 2.8.x the implicit match method is dropped and the rule silently becomes an exact compare. Confirmed twice here now, on 2.8.1 and 2.8.3
a login with no registration route: the way in is the query behind it or the credentials inside it, and a 3-way response (success redirect / invalid / server error) is already a boolean oracle
a short second factor whose pending state is not bound to a cookie: it is shared server-side, so it can be attacked from any connection and re-armed at will by logging in again
known_traps: curl collapses /./ and // client-side unless --path-as-is is passed, so the bypass silently fails to fire and reads as a dead end. Pass it on every probe in this family.
/auth//login is NOT a bypass here: Werkzeug merges the duplicate slash and answers 308, so a redirect-following client reports the 403 it was redirected into. Only the LEADING double slash works.
/AUTH/LOGIN answers the Flask 404, so case variation is not a bypass -- Werkzeug routes are case-sensitive. Do not spend probes on it.

the boolean oracle needs the comment form. username="admin' AND '1'='1" answers 400 because the password clause survives, which looks like the injection failing; it is the injection working with a wrong payload shape. Use "admin' AND (<predicate>)--". Source: blueprints/login.py:28 interpolates BOTH fields into one f-string.

python's urllib RAISES the 302 as an HTTPError when a redirect handler declines the redirect, so the TRUE case of the oracle arrives in the except branch and a naive `r.status == 302` check reports every row as FALSE. This cost a full extraction run before it was caught.

the pending login has no cookie: blueprints/login.py:13 puts the code in ONE global uwsgi cache key with a 300s TTL, so it is per-instance state shared by everyone, and verify2fa.py:8 redirects to /auth/login whenever the key is absent. A brute-forcer whose success test is merely 'not 400' reads that 302 as a hit. Test for the real success shape (302 to /dashboard, or a Set-Cookie) and re-login when the /auth/login redirect appears.

a redirect-following client makes that lapse look like something else entirely: the 302 leads to /auth/login, which the proxy denies, so the client reports 403 and you start hunting a WAF. An early run of this measurement produced 30x403 for exactly that reason and said nothing about what it was testing.

immediately after the correct code is accepted, concurrent in-flight attempts answer 500 rather than 400. verify2fa.py:26 calls uwsgi.cache_get(...).decode() after line 29 has already deleted the key, so the racing request passes cache_exists and then dereferences None. Three codes adjacent to the real one answered 500 in this solve; none of them was valid.
one isolated 403 in the middle of a brute-force run is the proxy, not a hit. Re-test any candidate serially before believing it.

measure a rate limit with a CONCURRENT burst and a control in the same run. Fired serially, 30 requests never filled the 60s sliding window and the control produced no 429 at all, which would have credited the bypass with an effect it had not been shown to have. The controls that make the result mean anything are: the same burst without the bypass, and a second no-bypass burst afterwards proving the bucket was still hot.

the X-Forwarded-For must still be a well-formed IPv4 when the ACL does match: haproxy.cfg:24-26 denies with 400 on anything the regex rejects, so 'not-an-ip' and 999.1.1.1 both answer 400 and look like an application response.
